title: The Permanent Seat and UN Reform

cards.h: Why a rising power wants a permanent seat
cards.b:
The UN Security Council (UNSC) still reflects 1945. Five permanent members (P5: US, UK, France, Russia, China) hold a veto. Africa and Latin America have no permanent seat. India, with 1.4 billion people, a top-five economy and a record of peacekeeping, has none either.

The campaign for a permanent seat is a pillar of Indian foreign policy. It has been pursued since the 1990s and, as of 2026, has not succeeded. Every year the UN General Assembly decides to continue talks.

Exam questions ask for the case for reform, the competing models, the obstacles (Article 108 and the P5), and what India should do.

• Article 23: the Council has 15 members: five permanent plus ten elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. The list was written into the Charter in 1945 (11 members). The General Assembly enlarged it to 15 in 1963 (Resolution 1991 (XVIII)), effective 1965. Nothing has changed since.
  • Article 24: the Council has primary responsibility for peace and security.
  • Article 27: nine affirmative votes are needed, including all five permanent members on non-procedural matters (the veto).
  • Articles 108 and 109: amendments need two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of members including all five permanent members. So any P5 state can block reform.

India has served as an elected member eight times: 1950–51, 1967–68, 1972–73, 1977–78, 1984–85, 1991–92, 2011–12 and 2021–22.

A 1979 General Assembly item on 'equitable representation' started the debate. In 1993 an Open-ended Working Group was formed. In 2005 Kofi Annan's report In Larger Freedom offered Models A and B. The 2005 World Summit pledged early reform, but no deal followed. Since 2009 the process runs as Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) in the General Assembly, based on Decision 62/557.

A decision in 2015 passed a 'framework document' to the IGN. Talks have been repetitive, with positions stated but no negotiating text.

• G4 (2004): six new permanent seats (two for Africa) and four more non-permanent. Veto issue deferred. Supports each other's claims.
  • African Union (Ezulwini Consensus 2005, Sirte Declaration): two permanent seats with full veto for Africa and five non-permanent.
  • Uniting for Consensus (UfC): led by Italy and Pakistan. Wants a larger Council of elected members only, with longer terms, no new permanent seats.
  • L.69 group: India co-leads this alliance of developing states (it takes its name from a 2007 draft resolution, A/61/L.69).
  • Small island states and others: want a seat rotation.

• Population and economy: the most populous country and one of the largest economies. India overtook Japan in nominal GDP in 2025 (IMF estimates).
  • Peacekeeping record (see the previous lesson).
  • Democratic, nuclear-armed and responsible, with a record of global public goods (ISA, vaccines).
  • Representation: the Council over-represents Europe and under-represents Africa, Asia and Latin America.
  • Legitimacy: a Council from 1945 cannot guide a 2026 world. Indian leaders call the present Council outdated and unrepresentative and urge 'reformed multilateralism'.

Support: France, the UK, Russia and the US have said they back India's permanent membership in some form. President Obama said in the Indian Parliament in 2010 that he looked forward to a reformed Council with India as a permanent member. China's language is vague: it says it understands India's aspirations but does not endorse them.

• The P5 veto over reform (Article 108). Each has its own interests.
  • China: does not want a rival Asian permanent member. It links itself to Japan and India separately.
  • Rivals: Pakistan (with Italy) in UfC, South Korea, Mexico, Argentina and Indonesia, who resist regional leaders.
  • African unity: the AU wants veto for Africa. Other groups reject new vetoes. The 2005 G4 draft put off the veto question for 15 years. India's later line is that if the veto stays, new permanent members should not be second-class.
  • Process: the IGN works by consensus and has no negotiating text.
  • Great-power politics: the US and others slow the talks.

• The General Assembly decided without a vote to continue the IGN in its 80th session and to put the item on the agenda of the 81st session (2026–27).
  • India's line (2026): start text-based negotiations with milestones and timelines. Expand both permanent and non-permanent categories. In the October 2026 IGN debate on the veto, India said the veto should not remain exclusive to the current five, and rejected a separate category of permanent seats, with or without a veto.
  • Pact for the Future (September 2024): for the first time a major UN outcome document committed states to Council reform.
  • Context: the Ukraine war, the Gaza war and the 2026 Iran war showed the Council's paralysis.
  • In 2022 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 76/262, requiring a debate after any veto. It is called the veto initiative.

Realists such as Mearsheimer say institutions reflect power and the P5 will not give it up. Liberals argue that legitimacy gaps will push states to build other forums. India's strategy is to hold both: press for reform but also invest in groups where it already has a seat (G20, BRICS, SCO, Quad).

Some Indian analysts suggest India should join reform packages that put off the veto question or add a review clause, rather than wait for a perfect deal.

• Build a stronger coalition with Africa (the AU seat in the G20 helps).
  • Seek P5 support in writing and press China directly.
  • Keep strong peacekeeping, development and disaster relief records.
  • Use non-permanent terms (2021–22) to show leadership. Consider a new elected term.
  • Link reform to the wider push to change the IMF, World Bank and WTO.

For the exam, keep a short table: Group, demand, India's stand. Cite Article 108 and the 1963 enlargement.

"India's quest for a permanent seat in the UNSC: assess the prospects." (typical)
"Why is UN reform so difficult? What can India do?" (typical)
"Discuss the proposals for UNSC expansion." (typical)

Structure: (1) structure and the 1945 hangover; (2) Articles 23, 27, 108; (3) reform history and groups (G4, UfC, AU); (4) India's claim; (5) obstacles; (6) 2024–26 developments (Pact for the Future, IGN stalemate); (7) way forward.

quiz.q: The Security Council was enlarged from 11 to 15 members in:
Which Article lets the P5 block Charter amendments through ratification?
quiz.w: Articles 108 and 109 require ratification by two-thirds including all P5.

quiz.q: The G4 comprises India, Brazil, Japan and:
The Uniting for Consensus group is led mainly by Italy and:
quiz.w: Pakistan, also Canada, Spain, Argentina and others.

quiz.q: The African Union's common position on UNSC reform is called the:
How many times has India been an elected UNSC member through 2022?
The IGN on Security Council reform has been running since:

o: A debate in the Assembly after any veto
quiz.w: The 'veto initiative' mandates a GA debate within 10 working days of a veto.

quiz.q: Which 2024 document first committed UN members to reform the Security Council in a major outcome text?
quiz.w: The Pact for the Future, September 2024.

quiz.q: Which leader declared in the Indian Parliament in 2010 that he looked forward to India as a permanent member?
